question: A 14-year-old girl comes to the physician for exertional leg pain. The pain began last week when she started jogging to lose weight. She is at the 5th percentile for height and 80th percentile for weight. Physical examination shows a broad neck with bilateral excess skin folds that extend to the shoulders, as well as a low-set hairline and ears. There is an increased carrying angle when she fully extends her arms at her sides. Pulses are palpable in all extremities; lower leg pulses are delayed. Which of the following additional findings is most likely in this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Broad neck with excess skin folds" -> "Turner syndrome" -> "Ovarian dysgenesis" -> 95%
CHAIN: "Increased carrying angle" -> "Cubitus valgus" -> "Turner syndrome" -> "Ovarian dysgenesis" -> 85%
CHAIN: "Delayed lower leg pulses" -> "Possible coarctation of the aorta" -> "Turner syndrome" -> "Ovarian dysgenesis" -> 80%
enhanced_information: The clinical presentation of the 14-year-old girl, including a broad neck with excess skin folds, short stature, increased carrying angle (cubitus valgus), and delayed lower leg pulses, is highly suggestive of Turner syndrome. Turner syndrome is characterized by features such as ovarian dysgenesis, which is the most likely additional finding in this patient. The retrieved evidence paths support the association between Turner syndrome and cardiovascular manifestations, such as coarctation of the aorta, which can explain the delayed lower leg pulses. Therefore, the consensus-aligned reasoning indicates that ovarian dysgenesis is the most likely additional finding in this patient with Turner syndrome.
analysis: The clinical presentation of the 14-year-old girl is highly indicative of Turner syndrome, a condition characterized by a 45,X karyotype. Key features of Turner syndrome include short stature, a broad neck with excess skin folds (webbed neck), low-set ears, and a low hairline. The increased carrying angle (cubitus valgus) and delayed lower leg pulses suggest possible cardiovascular involvement, such as coarctation of the aorta, which is common in Turner syndrome. One of the hallmark findings in Turner syndrome is ovarian dysgenesis, leading to primary amenorrhea and infertility due to streak ovaries. This aligns with the clinical presentation and is the most likely additional finding. Other options, such as an absent uterus, mitral valve prolapse, triphalangeal thumb, and horseshoe adrenal gland, are not typically associated with Turner syndrome. Therefore, the most likely additional finding in this patient is ovarian dysgenesis.
